articles.title: Former Virginia Tech QB Pop Watson draws high praise that shouldn't surprise Hokies' fans
articles.excerpt: Former Virginia Tech quarterback Pop Watson drew high praise from his new coach at UMass ahead of their season opener on Thursday night.
articles.content:
When the Transfer Portal opened back in January, you knew that there were going to be some Virginia Tech players looking for a new home in 2026. It was inevitable. After James Franklin was hired, some players saw the writing on the wall and bolted for greener pastures.

One of those players was quarterback Pop Watson, who returned home to Massachusetts to play at UMass, a program that has nowhere to go but up. He committed to Virginia Tech while he was a star at Springfield Central High School. Now, he heads home, 30 minutes from his hometown, to take over as QB1 for the Minuteman. Head coach Joe Harasymiak didn't mince words about his new signal caller.

Former Virginia Tech QB Pop Watson draws praise ahead of UMass opener

It wasn't surprising that Watson transferred, and it wasn't surprising that he returned home to continue his career. During his time in Blacksburg, he sat behind Baylor transfer Kyron Drones, but he played a big role in the Hokies becoming bowl-eligible in 2024. After Drones and UCLA transfer Collin Schlee went down with injuries in November that year, that left former head coach Brent Pry with Watson to play the season finale against Virginia in Blacksburg.

Watson was good, going 14-for-21 for 254 yards through the air and a touchdown in the Hokies' 37-17 rout of the Cavaliers to retain the Commonwealth Cup. He also rushed for 48 yards on 11 carries and a touchdown as the Hokies ended up in the Duke's Mayo Bowl in Charlotte against Minnesota that year. It was his ability to progress through his reads against Virginia's defense and have a near-perfect day that Virginia Tech needed. Now, he'll get his shot to run his own offense beginning on Thursday night on the road against Rutgers in the Big Ten. Harasymiak dropped a quote that should get Minutemen fans excited after a 0-12 2025 season.

“This goes from the pros on down: You have to have a dude at that spot,” Harasymiak said, per Amin Touri of the Boston Globe. “The best thing about recruiting is when both parties align on what they want. . . . We needed a quarterback. Bad. Our quarterback play was atrocious last year. No leadership. It was a revolving door. Gave everybody an opportunity. Didn’t happen.

“We know we need to fix that. We feel like we’ve done that.”

Read More: Former Virginia Tech QB Pop Watson delivers a stunning message to UMass fans

UMass does have that "dude'' for the MAC with Watson, who was a fan favorite in Blacksburg and even had fan support the last couple of years when Drones struggled, and fans wanted his name called. It never really was, and that's too bad. Franklin has brought in Penn State transfer Ethan Grunkemeyer to be his starter in Blacksburg, as well as North Carolina transfer Bryce Baker. Redshirt freshman Kelden Ryan and true freshman Troy Huhn have also impressed in fall camp in what is a very young room for the ACC. The Hokies also have four-star Class of 2027 quarterback Peter Bourque from Hingham, Mass., committed for the future.

The future is bright for the quarterback room at Virginia Tech, but it is also high for Watson, who has a chance to become a hero in Amherst and help the program turn around in 2026. UMass is a perfect spot for Watson, and his journey begins against Rutgers Thursday night.

articles.title: Boeing finds US$1.9 billion hole after bringing Spirit AeroSystems back in-house, report says
articles.excerpt: Unexpected costs from the US$8.4 billion acquisition are weighing on Boeing Commercial Airplanes as the manufacturer works to increase 737 MAX and 787 production
articles.content:
Boeing has found that the liabilities inherited with its acquisition of Spirit AeroSystems exceed identifiable assets by approximately US$1.9 billion, adding an unexpected financial burden as the US manufacturer works to accelerate production of the 737 MAX and 787.

The figure was calculated by The Wall Street Journal from Boeing's financial disclosures following the completion of the Spirit acquisition in December 2025. Boeing agreed to bring its former supplier back in-house primarily to gain greater control over manufacturing and quality, particularly on the 737 program.

The newspaper's analysis shows that the financial consequences have become considerably larger than initially apparent. Boeing valued the total consideration for Spirit at US$8.39 billion, including shares issued to Spirit stockholders, previous advances and debt assumed or repaid as part of the transaction.

Boeing's own second-quarter filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission provides further evidence of the costs it inherited.

Follow Air Data News: WhatsApp | Instagram | LinkedIn | Twitter | Facebook

The company has provisionally assigned US$10.28 billion in goodwill to the Spirit acquisition, up from an initial estimate of approximately US$10 billion. Goodwill is an accounting asset that, in this case, largely results from the value of the business exceeding the net value of the identifiable assets and liabilities acquired.

More significant for Boeing's aircraft business are the liabilities behind that calculation. Accrued liabilities associated with Spirit increased from US$1.78 billion in December to US$2.20 billion by the end of June.

That includes US$1.52 billion related to what Boeing describes as "off-market customer contracts" — agreements whose economic terms are less favorable than those that could be obtained under current market conditions.

The accounting remains provisional. Boeing said valuations involving goodwill, off-market contracts and other accrued liabilities were still being assessed. The acquisition accounting period can continue for up to one year after the December 8, 2025 closing.

Spirit costs reach Boeing's aircraft business

The implications extend beyond Boeing's balance sheet because Spirit was deeply embedded in the production of several commercial aircraft programs.

Its Wichita operation builds the fuselage of the 737, making the former supplier an essential component of Boeing's effort to increase MAX production. Spirit also supplied major structures for the 787.

Before the acquisition, Spirit had repeatedly recorded forward losses on aircraft programs when estimated production costs exceeded the revenue expected under existing contracts.

In the third quarter of 2025 alone, Spirit recorded US$585 million in additional forward losses, primarily involving the Boeing 737 and 787 as well as the Airbus A220 and A350 programs. Higher production and supply-chain costs were among the reasons cited.

Some Airbus-related operations were transferred separately to the European manufacturer as part of the breakup of Spirit, meaning Boeing did not simply absorb the supplier in its entirety. But the acquisition brought important Boeing programs and their associated economic problems directly onto the manufacturer's books.

Those costs are already affecting expectations for Boeing Commercial Airplanes. Chief Financial Officer Jay Malave said in March that the commercial aircraft division was expected to approach breakeven margins in 2026 and become profitable in 2027, later than Boeing had previously anticipated. Higher-than-expected costs associated with Spirit were among the factors behind the outlook.

The commercial aircraft division recorded a US$632 million loss in 2025, after losing more than US$2 billion a year earlier.

Producing more aircraft is still essential

The additional costs arrive as Boeing needs substantially more aircraft to move through its factories.

The manufacturer has been rebuilding 737 MAX production after years of disruption caused by quality problems, supply-chain constraints and regulatory intervention. Higher deliveries are also essential to generate cash and reduce Boeing's debt.

That makes slowing production to contain Spirit-related costs an unattractive option. Boeing instead needs to lower the cost of producing structures inherited from Spirit while simultaneously increasing output.

The situation creates an unusual short-term challenge. Some of the work brought inside Boeing is associated with contracts and production economics that Spirit had already identified as unfavorable. Increasing production can therefore increase the amount of work performed under those conditions before efficiency improvements fully take effect.

Higher volumes, however, can also improve economics by spreading fixed costs across more aircraft. Boeing can now reorganize manufacturing, quality inspections and supply arrangements without the commercial boundary that previously separated it from Spirit.

That industrial control was one of the principal reasons for reversing a decision Boeing made two decades ago.

Boeing sold its Wichita structures operation in 2005, creating the business that became Spirit AeroSystems. The relationship came under intense scrutiny following the January 2024 Alaska Airlines 737 MAX 9 accident, when a door plug separated from an aircraft that had left Boeing's factory without four required retaining bolts.

Boeing announced its plan to reacquire Spirit later that year, arguing that bringing the companies together would align their production systems and safety and quality management.

737 and 787 face production increases

The 737 is particularly exposed to the success of that integration because every increase in final assembly requires a corresponding increase in fuselage production at Wichita.

Boeing is working toward higher MAX production rates and has also prepared an additional assembly line at its Everett facility in Washington state. Stabilizing the flow of fuselages from Wichita while reducing defects and rework is therefore central to increasing deliveries.

The 787 presents another challenge. Spirit had accumulated losses associated with its work on the Dreamliner before the acquisition, including US$167 million in additional forward losses recorded in the fourth quarter of 2024 alone.

Boeing is simultaneously increasing 787 production at its North Charleston, South Carolina, plant as demand for widebody aircraft remains strong.

The manufacturer therefore faces the task of extracting costs from the former Spirit operations without undermining quality or disrupting the production increases that motivated the acquisition in the first place.

Limited impact on aircraft prices in short term

The newly identified liabilities do not mean airlines should expect Boeing to simply increase the price of the 737 MAX or 787 to recover the costs.

Thousands of aircraft in Boeing's backlog were sold under contracts negotiated years ago, with pricing and escalation mechanisms already established. Unexpected manufacturing costs primarily reduce the margin Boeing earns from delivering those aircraft.

The US$1.52 billion valuation attached to off-market contracts does, however, demonstrate how unfavorable some inherited commercial arrangements have become compared with present market conditions.

That could provide Boeing with an incentive to seek better terms in future contracts and exercise greater discipline when pricing new aircraft orders.

The current commercial aircraft market provides some leverage. Both Boeing and Airbus have extensive backlogs, while production constraints mean delivery positions for many models are scarce for several years

articles.title: Following Nintendo's example, Sony and Microsoft argue they have no obligation to pass tariff refunds onto customers
articles.excerpt: Microsoft, Sony and Nintendo are in agreement that you shouldn't expect refunds for paying extra for their products as a result of US tariffs.
articles.content:
"Paying fair market price for voluntarily purchased consumer goods is not a legally cognisable injury."

Lawyers representing Sony and Microsoft have argued, in two separate lawsuits, that the platform holders are not obligated to pass tariff refunds back to consumers. Sony and Microsoft have had to raise prices of their PlayStation and Xbox consoles in 2025 in response to US-imposed tariffs. The US Supreme Court ruled the tariffs illegal earlier this year, allowing impacted companies to request refunds.

Both Sony and Microsoft will receive refunds, but consumers who paid higher prices for their products as a result of the tariffs will not be compensated. As reported by Game File, the two companies are being sued separately by affected consumers who say they should receive refunds.

In Sony's case, brought against it by a group of players in California, the company used a familiar line of argument that essentially said consumers got what they paid for.

"Paying fair market price for voluntarily purchased consumer goods is not a legally cognisable injury in fact," Sony argued in a legal motion. The company is seeking to dismiss the suit early before it could turn into a class-action lawsuit.

Microsoft's case was initiated by one individual in Washington State, who is likewise seeking a refund. Once again, the company's argument against the suit is familiar.

"There is nothing unjust about Plaintiff purchasing an Xbox at an advertised price and getting exactly what he paid for - regardless of whatever theory he devised months later about Microsoft's cost structure," Microsoft's lawyers argued.

"Plaintiff provides no specific allegations that would establish any pricing differential attributable to tariffs or suggest any possibility that Microsoft applied then or could recreate now any dollar-for-dollar calculation of tariff-related pricing - any more than it could any other market factor that affects pricing," Microsoft's argument went on.

It's notable that neither Sony nor Microsoft directly named tariffs as the reason they're raising console prices. When Sony raised PlayStation 5 prices in August 2025, the company cited "a challenging economic environment". Microsoft's Xbox price hikes in May of the same year came alongside a statement about "market conditions and the rising cost of development".

The arguments echo those made by Nintendo, who's facing its own lawsuit about the same claim. Nintendo also said in July that it was under no obligation to pass tariff refunds to consumers who bought Switch consoles at elevated prices.

In all cases, consumers are frustrated that companies get paid twice, once by those who buy the price-hiked consoles and another when tariffs are refunded. In July, Sony told investors it's expecting $508m (£375m) in tariff refunds from the US government, with most of that going to PlayStation. Indeed, none of the three companies have lowered prices in response to the tariffs getting struck down, meaning they will continue to benefit from the elevated prices. In all lawsuits, a judge has yet to rule in favor of the arguments made by Sony, Microsoft or Nintendo, as Game File notes.

Though the big three may be adamant they don't owe consumers any refunds, some companies are passing the refunds back to their customers. Playdate maker Panic recently announced anyone who bought its handheld console while the tariffs were in effect will be refunded the difference. Earlier in August, PC cooling company Arctic promised to do the same, and reduce the prices of its products for a period of time, too.

articles.title: Tesla readies Cybercab launch event shrouded in mystery
articles.excerpt: Tesla Inc. is set to reintroduce the purpose-built driverless car at a launch event Thursday in Austin, this time to formally add it to the company's robotaxi service.

(Bloomberg) — In late 2024, Elon Musk took the stage on a Hollywood studio lot to unveil the Cybercab, a vehicle with no steering wheel or foot pedals that he promised would revolutionize car travel across the country. 

Almost two years later, he’s about to do something similar again.

Tesla Inc. is set to reintroduce the purpose-built driverless car at a launch event Thursday in Austin, this time to formally add it to the company’s robotaxi service. The vehicle, which has been in testing in multiple US cities in recent months, is seen as a key piece of Tesla’s plan to evolve beyond a maker of electric vehicles into a pioneer of artificial intelligence products.

Musk, the automaker’s chief executive officer, touted the car in a series of overnight X posts ahead of the event, including one saying simply, “A storm of Cybercabs.”

Yet key questions remain unanswered ahead of the invite-only event for Tesla fans and social media influencers. It’s unclear, for example, whether the company plans to immediately deploy the vehicles for broad commercial service, or take a more measured approach, such as by offering demonstration rides in specific areas.

“If Thursday’s event is merely an unveiling with limited vehicles committed to the road, we expect the stock to sell off,” Andrew Percoco, a Morgan Stanley analyst, said in a note. “Conversely, a broader rollout that has a material impact on the Tesla robotaxi fleet size” could excite investors.

Tesla’s stock could use a boost, having fallen 21% this year through Wednesday, while the S&P 500 Index rose 12%. The company’s shares have rallied somewhat in the weeks leading up to the event, rising 20% since July 29.

Musk has pitched the Cybercab as the eventual backbone of a vast Tesla robotaxi fleet reaching most of the US, vowing to deploy thousands of the cars.

That grand vision has yet to materialize. Using versions of its Model Y SUV, Tesla began its long-awaited autonomous ride-hailing service last year in Austin and has since grown to six cities in Texas and Florida. In some instances, the rides include human safety monitors in the vehicle.

The company had registered 45 Cybercabs with authorities in Texas as of late Wednesday. That suggests Tesla is preparing for a larger-scale rollout, Percoco said. 

With the Cybercabs, Tesla’s Texas fleet consists of 420 robotaxis, mostly Model Y vehicles. That’s less than half of the nearly 1,000 vehicles that Alphabet Inc.’s Waymo, the leader in the robotaxi market, has registered in Texas.

Regulatory Issues

Uncertainty surrounding the event extends to the Cybercab itself: It’s unclear how Tesla has approached potential regulatory hurdles posed by the Cybercab’s lack of traditional driver controls.

Federal rules typically require all vehicles to have several human-centric design features such as a brake pedal and side mirrors. Although US auto safety regulators have proposed changes to remove unnecessary barriers for autonomous cars, those plans have not been finalized.

Tesla also hasn’t followed the same path as Zoox, Amazon.com Inc.’s autonomous vehicle unit. The company in July secured an exemption from several federal safety standards to allow the commercial deployment of its own purpose-built robotaxi. The exemption was granted after Zoox faced issues attempting to self-certify its vehicle as compliant with federal motor vehicle standards.

As of Wednesday, Tesla had not filed an exemption request for the Cybercab with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. The agency said it’s in touch with the company and monitoring the situation.

articles.title: Beating the summer heat in September: The signs first responders are warning of
articles.excerpt: During peak summer months, Wake County EMS responded to about 15 calls a day for heat-related illness. This week, they're preparing for another stretch of dangerous heat.
articles.content:
• Related
  • heat
  • EMS
  • first responders
  • severe weather

September may be here, but dangerous summer-like heat is sticking around across central North Carolina and health officials say the impact of this year's heat may be greater than the numbers show.

North Carolina recorded 5,861 heat-related emergency department visits between May 1 and Sept. 2, according to Autumn Locklear Clark, climate and health epidemiologist for the North Carolina Division of Public Health.

Other WRAL Top Stories

The heat is also keeping Wake County first responders on alert.

“Going in September, people may think, ‘Oh! We’re past the summer months,’ but September is still expected to be hot,” said Staten Young, commander and assistant chief of community outreach for Wake County.

The Triangle is facing several days of intense, near-record heat, with temperatures climbing into the upper 90s and heat index values potentially reaching 105 degrees or higher.

The intense heat is expected to continue through Friday.

The late-season heat is unusual historically. Since 1887, Raleigh has recorded only 16 September days with temperatures at or above 99 degrees.

But longer-term data show fall is getting warmer.

Raleigh's average fall temperature has increased 2.9 degrees since 1970, according to Climate Central. Fall temperatures have warmed in 98% of the U.S. cities analyzed by the organization.

Nearly 5,900 heat-related emergency visits in North Carolina

North Carolina's forthcoming heat surveillance report includes 5,720 heat-related emergency department visits through Aug. 29, the state's most recently completed reporting period. That number had increased to 5,861 by Sept. 2.

The state's highest weekly rate this summer came between June 28 and July 4, when North Carolina recorded 7.7 heat-related emergency department visits per 100,000 residents.

Working-age men between 25 and 44 and men 65 and older have consistently experienced some of the highest rates, according to Locklear Clark.

Wake County emergency responders have seen the consequences firsthand.

“There have been spikes through the summertime where we’ve had some days where it’s been as high as 15 calls,” Young said.

Health officials say the real impact could be higher

About 20% of North Carolina's heat-related emergency department visits are believed to be work-related, but state health officials consider that an underestimate.

Research also suggests heat-related deaths may be substantially undercounted nationally because extreme temperatures can worsen heart, kidney and respiratory conditions without heat ultimately appearing on a person's death certificate.

For people spending time outside, Young said preparation should begin before temperatures peak.

“You know you’re going to be sweating,” Young said. “You need to start hydrating the days before your practice even starts.”

Health officials recommend limiting strenuous outdoor activity during the hottest part of the day, drinking water regularly and taking breaks in cooler locations.

Wetting the skin or clothing can help the body release heat, and using a fan can increase evaporation. Immersing the hands and forearms in cool water can also help lower body temperature.

Heat stroke can cause confusion, fainting or seizures and requires immediate medical attention. Anyone showing signs of heat stroke should be cooled immediately while someone calls 911.

“Some of the key components that may happen with overheating and heat stroke is the potential for internal organ damage,” Young said.

For Raleigh resident Andy Masullo, keeping his family comfortable during the September heat meant sticking to the shade while his child enjoyed the park and splash pad.

“We’re in the shade, and it’s all about dancing around where you can,” he said.

With dangerous temperatures expected to persist through Friday, first responders say people should treat the September heat the same way they would during the height of summer.
